# Perinatal asphyxia and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Pediatrics > Neonatology > Perinatal asphyxia and hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy*

[Original Article Link](/library/h40cQT)

---

## Summary

<u>Perinatal asphyxia</u>, a common <u>cause of death</u> in <u>neonates</u>, is caused by compromised <u>placental</u> or pulmonary <u>gas exchange</u> and can occur during the antepartum, <u>intrapartum</u>, or <u>perinatal period</u>. Persisting impairment of <u>blood gas</u> exchange results in oxygen deficiency, <u>hypercapnia</u>, and blood <u>acidosis</u> with potential subsequent compromise of cell function in various tissues (e.g., <u>heart</u>, muscle, <u>brain</u>). The <u>brain</u> is the most vulnerable organ in the context of <u>perinatal asphyxia</u> and the development of <u>hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy</u> is a potential consequence. After rapid evaluation, eligible patients require <u>therapeutic hypothermia</u> over a period of 72 hours to minimize <u>brain damage</u>. Depressed <u>myocardial</u> function can exacerbate <u>ischemia</u> and cause subsequent short-term complications with <u>end-organ damage</u> in other tissues (e.g., <u>kidneys</u>, <u>lung</u>, <u>liver</u>, <u>gastrointestinal tract</u>, <u>bone marrow</u>). Long-term complications of <u>perinatal asphyxia</u> include irreversible neurological damage, <u>cerebral palsy</u>, and <u>periventricular leukomalacia</u>.

---

## Treatment

* <u>Therapeutic hypothermia</u> [[9]](/library/QfXuNx)

* Description

* Current <u>standard of care</u> for <u>neonates</u> with moderate to severe <u>HIE</u>

* Possible as selective head cooling or systemic <u>hypothermia</u>

* Treatment at 91.4–95 °F for 72 hours

* Within the first 6 hours of life (therapeutic window)

* Eligibility criteria

* <u>Gestational age</u> ≥ 36 weeks and ≤ 6 hours of age
PLUS

* <u>pH</u> ≤ 7 or <u>base deficit</u> of â¥ 16 mmol/L

* PLUS either of the following

* APGAR score at 10 min: ≤ 5
OR

* Ongoing resuscitation at 10 min
OR

* Clinically moderate or severe <u>encephalopathy</u>

* Supportive measures

* Ensure sufficient oxygenation and ventilation (e.g., <u>supplemental oxygen</u>, <u>inhaled nitric oxide</u>, <u>intubation</u>).

* Maintain adequate organ <u>perfusion</u> (e.g., <u>inotropic</u> agents).

* Maintain <u>electrolyte</u> and <u>glucose</u> <u>homeostasis</u>.

* Anticonvulsive treatment of <u>seizures</u>

* Recent studies indicate a neuroprotective effect of <u>erythropoietin</u> in <u>neonates</u> with <u>HIE</u>.  [[10]](/library/8fXOLx)





> [!WARNING]
> While maintaining adequate organ <u>perfusion</u> is important in children with <u>HIE</u>, <u>volume overload</u> should be avoided due to the possible subsequent development/worsening of <u>brain edema</u>.

---

## Complications

### <u>CNS</u> complications




* <u>Cerebral palsy</u> (most likely <u>spastic</u> <u>quadriplegia</u> or dyskinetic <u>cerebral palsy</u>)

* <u>Periventricular leukomalacia</u> (<u>PVL</u>)

* <u>Epilepsy</u>

* <u>Specific learning disorders</u>

* <u>ADHD</u>

* Intellectual developmental disorder

* <u>Hearing</u> and/or visual impairment





### Other organ complications




* <u>Heart</u>: impaired <u>myocardial contractility</u>

* <u>Kidneys</u>: <u>acute renal failure</u>

* Mainly <u>conservative treatment</u> necessary

* <u>Theophylline</u> has a nephroprotective effect [[11]](/library/f3Xk3B)

* Dialysis in rare cases

* Increased risk for the development of <u>chronic kidney disease</u> later in life

* <u>Hematopoietic</u>: <u>bone marrow suppression</u>, <u>thrombocytopenia</u>, <u>disseminated intravascular coagulation</u>

* <u>Liver</u>: <u>elevated transaminase</u> levels, hepatic injury

* <u>Gastrointestinal tract</u>: <u>necrotizing enterocolitis</u> in case of severe <u>hypoperfusion</u>

* <u>Lungs</u>: <u>neonatal respiratory distress syndrome</u>, <u>pulmonary hypertension</u>





We list the most important complications. The selection is not exhaustive.
